replacement: His main feeling was relief that the murderer was Mitya and not Smerdyakov, though you would have expected the reverse. He did not want to analyze why, and in fact felt a real repugnance at prying into his own feelings. He seemed to want to hurry up and forget something. Over the next few days he became convinced of Mitya’s guilt, as he learned how heavy the evidence against him was. Some of it came from unimportant people, Fenya and her mother for example, yet its effect was almost crushing. As for Perhotin, the people at the tavern and at Plotnikov’s shop, and the witnesses at Mokroe, their evidence looked conclusive. It was the details that did the damage. The secret of the knocks impressed the lawyers nearly as much as Grigory’s evidence about the open door. Grigory’s wife, Marfa, answering Ivan’s questions, declared that Smerdyakov had lain all night on the other side of the partition wall. “He was not three paces from our bed.” She was a sound sleeper, yet she had woken several times and heard him groaning. “He was groaning the whole time, groaning without a stop.”

“What is there left to tell? I was lying there, and I thought I heard the master shout. Just before that, Grigory Vassilyevitch had suddenly got up and gone out, and then he let out a scream, and after that it was all silent and dark. I lay there waiting, my heart thumping. I couldn’t stand it. In the end I got up and went out. The window on the left, the one facing the garden, was standing open. I stepped over to the left and listened for whether he was sitting in there alive, and I heard the master moving about and sighing. So I knew he was alive. ‘Ech!’ I thought. I went up to the window and called to him, ‘It’s me.’ And he called back, ‘He’s been here, he’s been here; he’s run off.’ He meant Dmitri Fyodorovitch had been. ‘He’s killed Grigory!’ ‘Where?’ I whispered. ‘There, in the corner,’ he said, and pointed. He was whispering too. ‘Wait a bit,’ I said. I went to the corner of the garden to look, and there was Grigory Vassilyevitch, lying by the wall, covered in blood and out cold. So it’s true, I thought, Dmitri Fyodorovitch really has been here. And on the spot I decided to put an end to it all. Grigory Vassilyevitch, even if he was alive, would never know what happened, lying there senseless like that. The one danger was that Marfa Ignatyevna might wake up. I felt that at the time. But the longing to get it done had come over me so badly that I could scarcely breathe. I went back to the window and told the master, ‘She’s here, she’s come; Agrafena Alexandrovna has come and wants to be let in.’ And he jumped like a baby. ‘Where is she?’ he gasped, but he couldn’t believe it. ‘She’s standing out there,’ I said. ‘Open up.’ He looked out of the window at me, half believing and half suspicious, and afraid to open. ‘Why, he’s afraid of me now,’ I thought. And it struck me as funny. So I thought of knocking on the window frame, right there before his eyes, with those taps we had agreed on as the sign that Grushenka had come. He didn’t seem to trust my word, but the moment he heard the taps, he ran to open the door. He opened it. I would have gone in, but he stood in the doorway so I couldn’t get past. ‘Where is she? Where is she?’ He stared at me, shaking all over. ‘Well,’ I thought, ‘if he’s that frightened of me, it looks bad!’ And my legs went weak with fear that he wouldn’t let me in, or would shout, or that Marfa Ignatyevna would come running, or that something else would go wrong. I can’t remember now, but I must have stood there pale, facing him. I whispered to him, ‘Why, she’s there, right under the window; how can you not see her?’ ‘Bring her, then, bring her.’ ‘She’s scared,’ I said; ‘the noise frightened her, she’s hiding in the bushes; go and call her yourself from the study.’ He ran to the window and put the candle on the sill. ‘Grushenka,’ he cried, ‘Grushenka, are you there?’ He cried it, but he wouldn’t lean out of the window, and he wouldn’t step away from me, because he was in a panic. He was so frightened he didn’t dare turn his back on me. ‘Why, there she is,’ I said. I went up to the window and leaned right out. ‘There she is; she’s in the bush, laughing at you, can’t you see her?’ All at once he believed it. He was shaking all over—he was terribly crazy about her—and he leaned right out of the window. I snatched up the iron paperweight from his table; you remember it, about three pounds in weight? I swung it and struck him on the top of the skull with the corner. He didn’t even cry out. He just sagged down, and I struck him again, and a third time. By the third blow I knew I had broken his skull. He suddenly rolled over on his back, face up, covered in blood. I looked round. There was no blood on me, not a spot. I wiped the paperweight and put it back. Then I went to the ikons, took the money out of the envelope, and flung the envelope on the floor with the pink ribbon beside it. I went out into the garden, shaking all over, straight to the apple tree with the hollow in it—you know the hollow. I’d marked it long before and left a rag and a scrap of paper ready inside. I wrapped all the notes in the rag and shoved it deep into the hole. And there it stayed for over two weeks. I took it out afterwards, when I came out of the hospital. I went back to my bed and lay down, thinking, ‘If Grigory Vassilyevitch has been killed outright, it may turn out badly for me. But if he’s not killed and he recovers, it’ll be first-rate, because then he’ll swear that Dmitri Fyodorovitch was here, and so Dmitri Fyodorovitch must have killed him and taken the money.’ Then I began to groan, from suspense and impatience, to wake Marfa Ignatyevna as soon as I could. At last she got up and ran to me, but when she saw that Grigory Vassilyevitch wasn’t there, she ran out, and I heard her scream in the garden. That set it all in motion, and it put my mind at rest.”

“Listen ...” said Ivan, who seemed bewildered again and was struggling to catch hold of something. “Listen. There are many questions I wanted to ask you, but I’ve forgotten them ... I keep forgetting, and I get muddled. Yes. Tell me this, at least. Why did you open the envelope and leave it lying on the floor? Why didn’t you just carry the envelope off?... When you were telling me, I thought you spoke of it as if it were the right thing to do ... but why, I can’t understand....”

“Allow me to ask,” the counsel for the defense began, with the friendliest and even respectful smile, “you are, of course, the same Mr. Rakitin whose pamphlet, _The Life of the Deceased Elder, Father Zossima_, published by the diocesan authorities, full of deep and religious reflections and opening with an excellent, devout dedication to the bishop, I have just read with such pleasure?”

No, I can never forget those moments. She began telling her story. She told everything, the whole episode that Mitya had told Alyosha, her bowing to the ground, and her reason for it. She told about her father and how she went to Mitya. Not in one word, not in a single hint, did she let on that Mitya himself, through her sister, had suggested that they “send Katerina Ivanovna” to fetch the money. She generously kept that back, and she was not ashamed to make it seem that she had run to the young officer on her own impulse, counting on something ... to beg him for the money. It was something tremendous! I went cold and trembled as I listened. The court was hushed, straining to catch each word. It was something without precedent. Even from a girl as willful and scornfully proud as she was, such a frank confession, such sacrifice, such self-immolation, seemed unbelievable. And for what, and for whom? To save the man who had deceived and insulted her, and to help, however little, in saving him, by making a strong impression in his favor. And indeed, the figure of the young officer who, with a respectful bow to the innocent girl, handed her his last four thousand roubles, all he had in the world, was cast in a very sympathetic and attractive light. But ... I had a painful misgiving in my heart! I felt that slander might come of it later (and it did, in fact, it did). All over town afterwards it was repeated, with spiteful laughter, that the story was perhaps not quite complete, that is, in the statement that the officer had let the young lady leave “with nothing but a respectful bow.” People hinted that something had been left out here.

“Gentlemen of the jury,” began the prosecutor, “this case has caused a stir all over Russia. But why should that surprise us? What is so especially horrifying in it for us? We are so used to such crimes! That is what is truly horrible: that such dark deeds no longer horrify us. What ought to horrify us is that we have grown so used to them, and not this or that single crime. What are the causes of our indifference, of our lukewarm attitude toward such deeds, toward such signs of the times, which are ominous for an unenviable future? Is it our cynicism? Is it the premature exhaustion of mind and imagination in a society that is sinking into decay in spite of its youth? Is it that our moral principles are shattered to their foundations, or perhaps that we have no such principles at all? I cannot answer such questions. Yet they are disturbing, and every citizen not only must, but ought to be troubled by them. Our newborn and still timid press has already done the public a good service, for without it we would never have heard of the horrors of unbridled violence and moral degradation that the press keeps bringing to the notice, not only of those who attend the new jury courts set up in the present reign, but of everyone. And what do we read almost every day? Of things beside which the present case grows pale and seems almost commonplace. But what matters most is that the majority of our national crimes of violence bear witness to a widespread evil, now so general among us that it is hard to fight against it.
